:::{#def-trace}

#### Trace

The **trace** of a $p \times p$ matrix $\matr{M}$
is the sum of its diagonal entries:

$$\operatorname{tr}(\matr{M}) \eqdef \sum_{i=1}^p M_{ii}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-trace}

#### The trace of a $2 \times 2$ matrix

$$
\operatorname{tr}\paren{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}} = 1 + 4 = 5
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-matrix-derivative}

#### Matrix derivative

For a scalar-valued function $f(\matr{X})$
of an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{X}$,
the **matrix derivative** is the $m \times n$ matrix
whose $(i,j)$ entry is the partial derivative of $f$
with respect to the $(i,j)$ entry of $\matr{X}$:

$$
\left[\deriv{\matr{X}} f\right]_{ij} = \deriv{X_{ij}} f
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-matrix-derivative}

#### The matrix derivative of a trace

Let $\matr{X}$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix and $f(\matr{X}) = \operatorname{tr}(\matr{X}) = X_{11} + X_{22}$
(@def-trace).
Then $\deriv{X_{ij}} f = 1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise, so:

$$
\deriv{\matr{X}} f = \matr{I}_2
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-matrix-product-matrix}

#### Matrix derivative of the trace of a matrix product

If $\matr{A}$ ($r \times m$) and $\matr{B}$ ($n \times r$)
are constant with respect to the $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{X}$,
then:

$$
\underbrace{\deriv{\matr{X}} \operatorname{tr}(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})}_{m \times n} =
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{A}}}_{m \times r}
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{B}}}_{r \times n}
$$

:::: notes
The trace makes $\operatorname{tr}(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})$ a scalar,
so its matrix derivative is again an $m \times n$ matrix.
The derivative of the matrix product $\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B}$ itself
(without the trace) is a fourth-order tensor,
which is why this result is stated for the scalar $\operatorname{tr}(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})$.
::::

:::

::: proof

Write $A_{kl}$, $X_{kl}$, and $B_{kl}$ for the entries of
$\matr{A}$, $\matr{X}$, and $\matr{B}$.
For entry $(i,j)$:

$$
\ba
\left[\deriv{\matr{X}} \operatorname{tr}(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})\right]_{ij}
&= \deriv{X_{ij}} \sum_{a=1}^{r} \sum_{b=1}^{m} \sum_{c=1}^{n} A_{ab} X_{bc} B_{ca}
&& \text{(trace of the } r \times r \text{ product } \matr{A}\matr{X}\matr{B} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{a=1}^{r} A_{ai} B_{ja}
&& \text{(only the terms with } b = i,\ c = j \text{ depend on } X_{ij} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{a=1}^{r} \left[\tp{\matr{A}}\right]_{ia} \left[\tp{\matr{B}}\right]_{aj}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= \left[\tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{B}}\right]_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-deriv-matrix-product-matrix}

#### Differentiating a weighted trace

Let $\matr{A} = \matr{I}_2$ ($2 \times 2$) and $\matr{B} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ ($2 \times 2$).
Then $\operatorname{tr}(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B}) = 2X_{11} + 3X_{22}$, and:

$$
\underbrace{\deriv{\matr{X}} \operatorname{tr}(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})}_{2 \times 2}
= \underbrace{\tp{\matr{A}}}_{2 \times 2} \underbrace{\tp{\matr{B}}}_{2 \times 2}
= \matr{I}_2 \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}
$$

:::
